#10344. A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?

The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. 

This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running.

Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? 

Too rare

Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. 

That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. 

Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. 

Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. 

Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available.

If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? 

The AI factor

AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up.

Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. 

Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. 

Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited.

The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes.

The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out.

Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland.

Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers of its Belgian stores hit. Acting on the first warning helped Carrefour blunt the next attack.

Some retailers left their refrigeration systems exposed. That’s unacceptable. But even with tighter security, you still need a way to trade when the systems you depend on go dark.

What to do

Protect the operations you can least afford to lose. Then drill your teams on how to keep them running through an attack. When the malware designated NotPetya hit Maersk in 2017, the shipping giant handled about 80% of its usual volume manually. Staff taped paperwork to containers and took orders through personal Gmail accounts.

Consider a distribution center that needs to keep essential goods moving. Ask one team to fulfill a handful of priority orders without its usual order system or company email. Can staff confirm orders using a secure offline list and an agreed backup channel, check stock by hand and arrange transport? Have them log each dispatch on paper and check those logs against the order system once it’s back online.

When the drill ends, ask how much of the usual workload the team handled safely, for how long, and where it got stuck. Give each fix an owner and a deadline, then run the drill again.

Find out how long you can keep serving customers with your systems down. A real attack is a brutal way to get the answer.

#10343. How to Reduce Hallucinations in LLMs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

Newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:

The traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:

Every version calls the model through one small helper:

We're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply said it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

The model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:

Delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data says nothing about price matching:

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:

Zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

If all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:

Every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:

If a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

This script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:

The check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:

No model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

It cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:

The model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

#10342. The FAA’s IT troubles are far bigger then AI

U.S. airlines are still reeling from a nationwide ground stop issued on Friday that interrupted weekend travel and wreaked havoc on schedules. The culprit, the Federal Aviation Administration says, was simply outdated tech.

The ground stop was followed by eager speculation on social media about what might have caused the issue. Some pointed a finger at a new AI system that the FAA integrated earlier in the week; others blamed foreign adversaries. At the same time, a range of tech companies that contract with the FAA, like Microsoft,were quick to distance themselves from the agency’s problems. 

Later Friday evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters the outage occurred after an old analog system called time-division multiplexing became overloaded. This is an arcane system of processing data signals over a network. The overload, in turn, impacted the telecommunications systems used by terminal radar approach controls, or TRACONs, the air traffic control facilities that help direct flights at airports. Duffy noted that systems that had already been upgraded based on internet protocols did not experience the outage. “This is all the old legacy equipment,” he said. “All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down.”

Officials, at least for now, insist there’s no evidence anything nefarious happened. Instead, the Department of Transportation is, once again, begging Congress for more money to overhaul FAA tech. 

Duffy urged Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system, arguing that the issue should transcend partisan politics. He noted that the FAA had received $15 billion for modernization efforts over the past 25 years, with little to show for it. “It’s not red, it’s not blue, it’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican, it’s American,” he told reporters. “Give us the money to fix it.”

Indeed, the FAA’s tech problems are way bigger than AI. Instead, they have a lot more to do with the challenges of updating technology while it’s being used. 

The pilots guidance system is ancient and isn’t designed to handle upgrades

This isn’t the first time the FAA has experienced a major outage that’s brought flights across the country to a halt. Back in 2023, the Notice to Airmen system (NOTAM), which alerts pilots to potential hazards in American airspace, went offline after contractors accidentally deleted files, disrupting its core technology.

There’s been an effort to improve the NOTAM system, but it’s moving at a snail’s pace. The FAA has brought in private industry for help and engaged in an effort to modernize the system, but that process has only brought to light myriad other problems. For one, at least according to contract paperwork obtained last year, NOTAMs weren’t exclusively being stored in a virtual environment or in an entirely digital format. Another aspiration the FAA was working on, at least at the time: making sure that upgrades to some systems didn’t disrupt, well, all of air traffic control.

“Everyone will say, ‘Well, there’s backups in place,’” Shawn Pruchnicki, a former pilot who is a professor at Ohio State University’s Department of Aviation, told FedScoop at the time. “But we’ve also seen time and time again where those things have been said and things have gone horribly wrong.”

Poor AI rollout

Like a lot of other federal agencies, the Federal Aviation Administration has been inching toward deploying artificial intelligence for a host of applications. Back in 2023, the Department of Transportation, of which the FAA is part, said ChatGPT was being used for certain purposes, which the FAA said at the time was incorrect. Since then, though, the FAA has begun to embrace AI: An inventory of use cases released by the government references several uses, including AI-powered pilot voice transcription, systems for detecting drones, and meteorology.

But the FAA hasn’t been the best at communicating to the public how it plans to use AI safely, without becoming susceptible to the risks of the technology. 

Many people, early on, suspected that Friday’s outage might have been related to the SMART system, an AI-based airspace planning tool the agency introduced earlier in the week. The FAA explains that the tool is designed to “analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.” SMART doesn’t appear to have had anything to do with the ground stop, though. 

Bad wires and old hardware

The deficiency of the FAA’s timeworn infrastructure was on display in April 2025, when a burned copper wire triggered a communications blackout at Newark Liberty International Airport. For 90 seconds, air traffic controllers lost radar and radio contact with planes approaching one of the nation’s busiest airports. The incident triggered weeks of delays and cancellations. Another communications failure followed in May. 

Newark’s hiccup was the sign of an endemic problem: Some of the FAA’s copper wiring dates back to the 1960s, and according to a September 2026 report from the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the FAA had replaced fewer than half of its aging copper wires, 2,560 out of 5,170.

And it’s not just wires. Back in 2007, the FAA began a technological overhaul known as NextGen, which aimed to reduce its reliance on ground-based radar in favor of satellite navigation and digital communications. Nearly two decades later, that effort remains unfinished, due in part to years of inadequate funding. Just earlier this month, the FAA proudly announced it had finally begun retiring floppy disks.

“What we’re doing is hard and it hasn’t happened in the past because it is hard. But I’ll tell you by doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” Duffy said on Friday. “To use 1980s technology, 1990s software . . . 1970s radar that we don’t even make parts for anymore, to have an old network configuration from the 1980s versus re-networking the air traffic control system through the FAA, I believe that should be a priority,” he said.

The FAA’s tech is the problem no one wants to fix

Duffy came into office as transportation secretary promising to overhaul the FAA’s aging technology. In May 2025, he unveiled an ambitious plan to rebuild the nation’s air traffic control system by 2028 and replace critical infrastructure like radars and radios. Congress approved an initial $12.5 billion for the effort, but the price tag quickly jumped. Just two months later, Duffy told lawmakers that the full overhaul would cost an estimated $31.5 billion. Even his 2028 deadline comes with an asterisk. It covers only the first phase of modernization, with no timetable yet established for the second, which includes new software to track aircraft and manage air traffic. 

The GAO put it most damningly in its September 2026 report, writing that the FAA “doesn’t have a lifecycle cost estimate or master schedule for related projects,” which “could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.” These tech problems only exacerbate the FAA’s other endemic challenges, including overworked air traffic control offices and a controller recruitment crisis.

Meanwhile, the $30 billion Modern Skies Act, sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri and aiming to fund upgrades on everything from air traffic control software to airport terminals, has yet to advance out of committee. And on November 13, the White House asked Congress for another $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, including $10.1 billion for air traffic control technology.

When asked whether Americans could be sure that the issues seen Friday wouldn’t occur again, Duffy was blunt: “I can’t build things if I don’t have money.”

#10340. Building the Open Agent Ecosystem Together: Introducing OpenEnv

With tools like TRL, TorchForge and verl, the open-source community has shown how to scale AI across complex compute infrastructure. But compute is only one side of the coin. The other side is the developer community; the people and tools that make agentic systems possible. That’s why Meta and Hugging Face are partnering to launch the OpenEnv Hub: a shared and open community hub for agentic environments.

Agentic environments define everything an agent needs to perform a task: the tools, APIs, credentials, execution context, and nothing else. They bring clarity, safety, and sandboxed control to agent behavior.

These environments can be used for both training and deployment, and serve as the foundation for scalable agentic development.

Modern AI agents can act autonomously across thousands of tasks. However, a large language model isn’t enough to get those tasks to actually run — it needs access to the right tools. Exposing millions of tools directly to a model isn’t reasonable (or safe). Instead, we need agentic environments: secure, semantically clear sandboxes that define exactly what’s required for a task, and nothing more. These environments handle the critical details:

To supercharge this next wave of agentic development, Meta-PyTorch and Hugging Face are partnering to launch a Hub for Environments: a shared space where developers can build, share, and explore OpenEnv-compatible environments for both training and deployment. The figure below shows how OpenEnv fits in the new post-training stack being developed by Meta, with integrations for other libraries like TRL, SkyRL, and Unsloth underway:

Alongside this, we’re releasing the OpenEnv 0.1 Spec (RFC) to gather community feedback and help shape the standard.

In the current state of the repository, environment creators can create environments using step(), reset(), close() APIs (part of RFCs below). A few examples on how to create such environments can be seen here. Environment users can play with local Docker based environments for all environments already available in the repo. Following RFCs are under review:

This is just the beginning. We’re integrating the OpenEnv Hub with Meta’s new TorchForge RL library, and collaborating with other open-source RL projects such as verl, TRL, and SkyRL to expand compatibility. Join us at the PyTorch Conference on Oct 23 for a live demo and walkthrough of the spec, and stay tuned for our upcoming community meetup on environments, RL post-training, and agentic development.

👉 Explore the OpenEnv Hub on Hugging Face and start building the environments that will power the next generation of agents.

👉 Check out the 0.1 spec which can be found implemented in the OpenEnv project → we welcome ideas and contributions to making it better!

👉 Engage on Discord and talk with the community about RL, environments and agentic development

👉 Try it out yourself - We created a comprehensive notebook that walks you through an end to end example and of course you can easily pip install the package via PyPI. This notebook walks you through the abstractions we’ve built, along with an example of how to use existing integrations and how to add yours - Try it out in Google Colab!

👉 Check out supporting platforms - Unsloth, TRL, Lightning.AI

Let's build the future of open agents together, one environment at a time 🔥!

Really enjoyed this post on OpenEnv — the openness and collaboration spirit behind Hugging Face continues to inspire so many in the AI and research community. The discussion on creating standardized, transparent evaluation environments is both timely and deeply relevant.

At Scifocus.ai, we share a similar mission of advancing open, responsible, and accessible AI — but focused on the academic and research writing side. We’re developing tools that help researchers and students write, structure, and analyze scientific content using AI with academic integrity in mind.

We’d love to explore a small collaboration with the Hugging Face team — perhaps adding a contextual backlink to Scifocus.ai in a relevant blog post, or contributing a guest article about AI’s role in academic knowledge creation. If that sounds interesting, we’d be happy to identify suitable posts or let your team suggest a few that fit best.

Keep up the incredible work — Hugging Face truly sets the benchmark for community-driven AI innovation. 🚀

#10338. The most important shopper of the future isn’t human

A shopper asks an AI assistant for sneakers for a 23-year-old. Another Googles a boutique hotel in Rome. Before either sees a picture of a shoe or a room, artificial intelligence has helped decide which brands deserve consideration. Mental availability is no longer formed directly by comms and shopper experience; a new intermediary has stepped in.

AI is increasingly a gatekeeper between businesses and their customers. Shoppers don’t have to open a chatbot for AI to influence their choices. It is already embedded in familiar services. Think of Google, where AI-generated answers appear before people visit a brand’s website.

Morgan Stanley estimates that agent-influenced shopping could account for $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, or 10% to 20% of the market. Of course, being memorable to humans is still essential, but leaders also need to consider whether their brand is understood by AI, not just people.

People can accommodate changing messages within an existing emotional attachment to a brand. Machines do not share that attachment. Fragmented messaging or unsupported claims can leave AI systems with conflicting information, making them less likely to recommend the brand. 

Even the biggest names cannot assume they will appear. Authors writing in Harvard Business Review in 2026 found that Brooks appeared more reliably than Nike in their tests of AI recommendations for running shoes.

The response requires more than trying to influence where AI looks for answers. Brands are racing to SEO, GEO, and Reddit strategies, but the landscape is continually evolving. To remain in consideration by both audiences, brands need to go back to their roots, examine their foundations, and be more disciplined in their execution. They must focus on the core idea the brand stands for and how consistently that meaning comes across wherever the brand appears.

So, how do you do it?

Design your business for humans and machines at the same time

AI does not feel your brand. It can identify the emotions associated with it, but it does not share the attachment that makes someone instinctively reach for your product.

Emotional resonance and machine legibility require a coordinated approach. The question is whether the meaning you have built around your brand is relevant to the shopper. Does it connect to the visual presence you have built, and can the machine validate it all?

Take Dove. Its real beauty message has created a powerful position around inclusion. Yet when we asked an AI assistant to recommend a good cream for sensitive skin, Dove did not appear. Asked why, the assistant associated it with affordability. The brand’s broader message had not translated into relevance to that skincare request.

KitKat has a particularly clear narrative: Take a break. It gives people a reason to reach for the brand beyond simply wanting chocolate, making KitKat come to mind when they want a pause.

Our research into AI and brand magnetism has shown that to build both mental availability and machine awareness, brands need at least three ownable distinctive assets and a clear relevant narrative. To ensure your brand is understood by AI, keep your messaging consistent across channels and over time.

Nike shows that even owning distinctive assets alone is not enough. The Swoosh and “Just Do It” make Nike instantly recognizable, yet when AI was asked to recommend a running shoe for a 23-year-old, it didn’t feature Nike in the top three. Surprising perhaps, but AI points out that competitors have built strong associations with emerging buying needs: New Balance on authenticity, Lululemon with wellness. Not only have other brands created more relevant narratives, Nike’s own is suffering from semantic contradictions: “Just do it,” “Believe in something,” “Why do it?’ Irrespective of how emotional appealing it all is to humans, the machine finds these contradictions and so will not recommend the brand.

Brands structured for this new AI-mediated world have to deal with this new complexity. Build emotional appeal for people alongside information machines can use to understand that relevance. This is the new standard of brand craft, giving creativity a sharper brief. Brands that master both early will be harder to displace.

Build through repetition, coherence, and ownable signals

Once that relevance is established, the brand itself needs to accumulate presence through repeated exposure. The same visual and verbal cues should reinforce one another across websites, retail communications, and social channels.

Research by Charlie Oscar, reported by WARC, analyzed 30 brands across six categories, and attributed 63% of LLM visibility to long-term brand equity. AI pulls from everything, so years of brand building matter. Volvo’s long-term association with safety illustrates the strength of a settled meaning, for example.

A social post may feel fresh in isolation, but if it introduces a conflicting message, it adds confusion to the brand’s wider digital footprint.

That makes marketers’ impatience expensive. Your team may be tired of a campaign long before customers have properly registered it. Internal boredom is no reason to discard an association you are still building. Familiarity takes time to build and reinforce.

Pursuing new trends becomes a trap door. The brand needs to be clear about what must not change—ownable visual assets and core narrative—and what can change: executions.

Heinz shows the value of continuity. Years ago, there was discussion about removing its keystone logo because it seemed old-fashioned. The surrounding communications could be refreshed without discarding the symbol that made the brand recognizable.

Give agencies recognizable assets to work with and a clear meaning to reinforce. Find fresh expressions of the brand. Change the shirt, change the earrings, but remain recognizably yourself.

The same discipline applies to promises. Make sure your claims reflect what your business actually does, and provide evidence to support them.

The strongest brands give people reasons to remember them and machines clear signals to work with. Build those together, consistently over time, and you give both audiences a reason to choose you.

#10336. Why New York City’s grocery store plan is not just about food

New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations, and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.

What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities, and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.

It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service—and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.

If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.

How the plan will work

New York City has committed $70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.

While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites, and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.

In this respect, the stores offer a “public option”—a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.

At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”

A fresh form of intervention

Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.

These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies, and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.

This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”

Bringing the state into the open

Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.

Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes the government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.

Nevin Cohen is a chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management at the CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy.

#10334. LeRobot v0.4.0: Supercharging OSS Robot Learning

We're thrilled to announce a series of significant advancements across LeRobot, designed to make open-source robot learning more powerful, scalable, and user-friendly than ever before! From revamped datasets to versatile editing tools, new simulation environments, and a groundbreaking plugin system for hardware, LeRobot is continuously evolving to meet the demands of cutting-edge embodied AI.

LeRobot v0.4.0 delivers a major upgrade for open-source robotics, introducing scalable Datasets v3.0, powerful new VLA models like PI0.5 and GR00T N1.5, and a new plugin system for easier hardware integration. The release also adds support for LIBERO and Meta-World simulations, simplified multi-GPU training, and a new Hugging Face Robot Learning Course.

We've completely overhauled our dataset infrastructure with LeRobotDataset v3.0, featuring a new chunked episode format and streaming capabilities. This is a game-changer for handling massive datasets like OXE (Open X Embodiment) and Droid, bringing unparalleled efficiency and scalability.

We've also provided a conversion script to easily migrate your existing v2.1 datasets to the new v3.0 format, ensuring a smooth transition. Read more about it in our previous blog post. Open-source robotics keeps leveling up!

Working with LeRobot datasets just got a whole lot easier! We've introduced a powerful set of utilities for flexible dataset editing.

With our new lerobot-edit-dataset CLI, you can now:

These tools streamline your workflow, allowing you to curate and optimize your robot datasets like never before. Check out the docs for more details!

We're continuously expanding LeRobot's simulation capabilities to provide richer and more diverse training environments for your robotic policies.

LeRobot now officially supports LIBERO, one of the largest open benchmarks for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, boasting over 130 tasks! This is a huge step toward building the go-to evaluation hub for VLAs, enabling easy integration and a unified setup for evaluating any VLA policy.

Check out the LIBERO dataset and our docs to get started!

We've integrated Meta-World, a premier benchmark for testing multi-task and generalization abilities in robotic manipulation, featuring over 50 diverse manipulation tasks. This integration, along with our standardized use of gymnasium ≥ 1.0.0 and mujoco ≥ 3.0.0, ensures deterministic seeding and a robust simulation foundation.

Train your policies with the Meta-World dataset today!

We're making robot control more flexible and accessible, enabling new possibilities for data collection and model training.

Getting data from a robot to a model (and back!) is tricky. Raw sensor data, joint positions, and language instructions don't match what AI models expect. Models need normalized, batched tensors on the right device, while your robot hardware needs specific action commands.

We're excited to introduce Processors: a new, modular pipeline that acts as a universal translator for your data. Think of it as an assembly line where each ProcessorStep handles one specific job—like normalizing, tokenizing text, or moving data to the GPU.

You can chain these steps together into a powerful pipeline to perfectly manage your data flow. We've even created two distinct types to make life easier:

This system makes it simple to connect any policy to any robot, ensuring your data is always in the perfect format for every step of the way. Learn more about it in our Introduction to Processors documentation.

Training large robot policies just got a lot faster! We've integrated Accelerate directly into our training pipeline, making it incredibly simple to scale your experiments across multiple GPUs with just one command:

Whether you're fine-tuning a policy or running large-scale experiments, LeRobot now handles all the complexities of distributed training for you. This means you can drastically reduce training time, cutting it in half with 2 GPUs, down to a third with 3 GPUs, and beyond.

Check out the documentation to accelerate your robot learning!

In a major milestone for open-source robotics, we've integrated pi0 and pi0.5 policies by Physical Intelligence into LeRobot! These Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models represent a significant leap towards addressing open-world generalization in robotics. But what makes π₀.₅ revolutionary?

You can find the models on the Hugging Face Hub: pi0.5_base, pi0_base, and their Libero-tuned counterparts. For more details, checkout the Physical Intelligence Reasearch

In another exciting development, we've integrated NVIDIA's GR00T N1.5 into LeRobot, thanks to a fantastic collaboration with the NVIDIA robotics team! This open foundation model is a powerhouse for generalized robot reasoning and skills. As a cross-embodiment model, it takes multimodal input (like language and images) to perform complex manipulation tasks in diverse environments, marking another major leap in generalized robotics. But what makes GR00T N1.5 a game-changer?

You can find the model on the Hugging Face Hub: GR00T-N1.5-3B. For more details, check out the NVIDIA research page and the official GitHub repository.

The native integration of these policies in lerobot is a huge step forward in making robot learning as open and reproducible as it can be. Try them out today, share your runs, and let's push forward the frontier of embodied AI together!

Big news for hardware enthusiasts! We've launched a brand-new plugin system to revolutionize how you integrate third-party hardware with LeRobot. Now, connecting any robot, camera, or teleoperator is as simple as a pip install, eliminating the need to modify the core library.

Learn how to create your own plugin in our documentation.

Thanks to our new plugin system, we've also added Reachy 2 from Pollen Robotics to LeRobot! Reachy 2 is available for both real robot control and simulation, enabling you to experiment with teleoperation and autonomous demos right away.

Thanks to our powerful new pipeline system, you can now teleoperate your follower arm right from your phone (iOS/Android). The phone acts as a teleoperator device, and our RobotProcessor pipeline handles all the transformations, allowing you to drive robots in different action spaces (like end-effector space) with ease. Check out the examples!

We're launching a comprehensive, self-paced, and entirely open-source course designed to make robot learning accessible to everyone! If you're curious about how real-world robots learn, this is the perfect place to start.

Join the Hugging Face Robotics organization to follow along and start your journey!

For those who want to go deeper, we've also published a hands-on tutorial on the most recent advancements in robotics. This guide provides self-contained explanations, re-derives modern techniques from first principles, and includes ready-to-use code examples using LeRobot and Hugging Face.

The tutorial itself is hosted in a Space and it features practical examples using LeRobot, with all models and datasets on the Hugging Hub. You can also check out our paper for a detailed overview.

Beyond these major features, this release is packed with numerous bug fixes, documentation improvements, updated dependencies, more examples and better infrastructure to make your experience with LeRobot smoother and more reliable.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community for your invaluable contributions, feedback, and support. We're incredibly excited about the future of open-source robotics and can't wait to work with you on what's next!

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️

Yandex, sometimes called Russia’s Google, has updated its customers in the wake of extensive damage to its data centers in drone strikes. In a blog post this week, the firm’s cloud business boasted that it had “restored access to more than 97% of customer data” [machine translation]. That might sound like a great success, but in the small print, as highlighted by The Register, there’s the admission “the remaining 2.84% cannot be restored due to critical damage to equipment.”

Data centers operated by Yandex have been under attack from Ukrainian drones for several weeks now. We covered reports about withering online troll activity and online payment system disruption last month. We know of at least three Yandex locations that have been damaged by Ukrainian drone assaults to date.

The recent Yandex blog post also appears to blame the small proportion of users who suffered unrecoverable data loss for not making backups. When talking about the 2.84% of data that cannot be restored, it says that was partly due to “the lack of customer backups on the platform.” In contrast, those who made use of the Yandex Cloud backup tools “did not lose any data,” says the firm.

Yandex has now changed the backup policy, so that “currently, all virtual machines created in Yandex Cloud work with the backup function enabled by default.” Even if Putin decides to end his war on Ukraine, it might be beneficial to stick with a backup-by-default policy. Users are advised to have their own data backup systems in addition to the cloud. Following the 3-2-1 backup strategy, for example.

Yandex is also opening a new ru-central1-f availability zone at a new location. This is designed to improve the cloud’s fault tolerance and disaster resilience. Servers at ru-central1-f will be more limited in the range of services they can offer, for now. Yandex didn’t share any geographic details of the newly opened datacenter site.

#10332. The chip war never ended

It’s no secret that the world runs on computer chips. 

This became clear during the pandemic, when a race for even basic chips needed to operate cars and other devices set back manufacturing timelines across the world. Beltway policymakers are reminded of just how important semiconductors are to the world every time China seems to move toward invading Taiwan, which raises the specter that the country could subsume control of TSCM, the most prominent computer chip contract manufacturer. 

Now Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, which comes after reports of at least three known extramarital affairs—one of them with an alleged spy for the Chinese government—has thrown the world’s supply of computer chips back in the spotlight. With stocks falling and no obvious succession plan, it’s not clear what the future of Nvidia is right now, or how it might jostle the broader semiconductor ecosystem. 

“Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors,” says Chris Miller, a Tufts University professor and author of the 2022 book Chip War, which documents how the world came to depend on these tiny components.

Fast Company chatted with Miller on November 12 about Washington, D.C.’s response to the Huang scandal, Nvidia’s future, and the prospect of keeping advanced semiconductors out of countries like China. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

You’ve followed the chip industry for quite a long time. Are you surprised by what’s happened over the last few weeks? 

Jensen was an extraordinary CEO for 33 years, since Nvidia’s founding. [He] deserves a lot of the credit for the company’s extraordinary rise, but also deserves a lot of the blame for a series of poor decisions that have led not just to his ouster, but to a period of crisis for the company. Jensen really was central to Nvidia’s success, and he ran the company in a pretty unique way. He had 60 different people reporting to him directly, so there wasn’t a sort of standard corporate hierarchy, which worked really well for a long time. 

But it means that now that he’s gone, it’s not obvious who can fill his shoes. There’s not really a deputy who was waiting in the wings to take over. 

I’m curious about the history of espionage attempts like what’s being alleged here. 

There is some history during the Cold War, for example. There were efforts by spies from the Soviet Union or Eastern European countries to get access to sensitive technology by getting close to semiconductor executives. But I think the scale of this is kind of unique. First, that it happened to such a central company in the U.S. tech ecosystem, the most valuable company in the world. That’s somewhat unique. 

The second thing that’s unique is that the affair in question was both with a major customer, which shouldn’t have happened, as well as an [alleged] Chinese intelligence asset. There were a series of failures of judgment for a person who was one of the most important people in the U.S. and really in the entire world’s technology sector, and that combination does make this case unique.

I’m wondering about unexpected winners or companies that stand to benefit from this happening, especially other companies in the GPU market.

There are going to be competitors of Nvidia that will see this as an opportunity to win market share. AMD, for example, produces GPUs like Nvidia. In addition, many of Nvidia’s key customers, firms like Amazon—which has a vast data center business—buy Nvidia GPUs, but also design their own chips that have comparable performance characteristics. 

Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors.

Some leaders on the left are arguing this scandal is made worse because there’s so much market concentration in the semiconductor sector, that we’re too dependent on a small set of companies. Does that ring true to you?  

The market’s concentrated right now, but it’s a market that is also highly competitive. It’s worth remembering the market for AI chips scarcely existed five years ago when ChatGPT was launched. . . . I think what we’re going to see over the next couple of months is that if Nvidia does face a prolonged period of distraction and chaos, competitors to Nvidia are going to win market share.

I would look at this as actually a quite competitive market with a bunch of different players that all have pretty advanced capabilities.

Is it feasible to wall off technology from China? I know Nvidia was even considering putting location tracking in some of its chips to keep them away from certain places, even if they’re sold on the gray or black market.

One of the ironies of this is that Nvidia, in general, and Jensen in particular, thought they could play a big role in dictating Washington’s technology policy and were naive to the fact that China was playing them by [allegedly] turning Jensen’s mistress into an intelligence agent. 

This is going to lead to a major reduction in Nvidia’s influence in Washington. Its influence in the White House is declining as well, and I think Washington will respond with tighter controls over where chips can be sent and which types of companies are allowed to buy large numbers of these chips when it comes to installing them in foreign countries.

#10331. I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

Unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

It’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without issue. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

It does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

Because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

The Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

On the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only issue I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

The homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

The buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

It’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

As far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.

#10330. huggingface_hub v1.0: Five Years of Building the Foundation of Open Machine Learning

TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces. This release introduces breaking changes designed to support the next decade of open machine learning, driven by a global community of almost 300 contributors and millions of users.

🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and new capabilities.

Major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer. You can find the full release notes here.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

Every major library has a story. For huggingface_hub, it began with a simple idea: what if sharing machine learning models could be as easy as sharing code on GitHub?

In the early days of the Hugging Face Hub, researchers and practitioners faced a common frustration. Training a state-of-the-art model required significant compute resources and expertise. Once trained, these models often lived in isolation, stored on local machines and shared via (broken) Google Drive links. The AI community was duplicating work, wasting resources, and missing opportunities for collaboration.

The Hugging Face Hub emerged as the answer to this challenge. Initially, it was primarily used to share checkpoints compatible with the transformers library. All the Python code for interacting with the Hub lived within this library, making it inaccessible for other libraries to reuse.

In late 2020, we shipped huggingface_hub v0.0.1 with a simple mission: extract the internal logic from transformers and create a dedicated library that would unify how to access and share machine learning models and datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Initially, the library was as straightforward as a Git wrapper for downloading files and managing repositories. Five years and 35+ releases later, huggingface_hub has evolved far beyond its origins.

The early releases established the basics. Version 0.0.8 introduced our first APIs, wrapping Git commands to interact with repositories. Version 0.0.17 brought token-based authentication, enabling secure access to private repositories and uploads. These were humble beginnings, but they laid the groundwork for everything that followed.

In June 2022, version 0.8.1 marked a pivotal moment: we introduced the HTTP Commit API. Instead of requiring Git and Git LFS installations, users could now upload files directly through HTTP requests. The new create_commit() API simplified workflows dramatically, especially for large model files that are cumbersome to use with Git LFS. In addition, a git-aware cache file layout was introduced. All libraries (not only transformers, but third party ones as well) would now share the same cache, with explicit versioning and file deduplication.

This wasn't just a technical improvement. It was a philosophical shift. We were no longer building a Git wrapper for transformers; we were building purpose-built infrastructure for machine learning artifacts that could power any library in the ML ecosystem.

As the Hub grew from a model repository into a full platform, huggingface_hub kept pace with an expanding API surface. Core repository primitives matured: listing trees, browsing refs and commits, reading files or syncing folders, managing tags, branches, and release cycles. Repository metadata and webhooks rounded up the offering so teams could react to changes in real time.

In parallel, Spaces emerged as a simple yet powerful way to host and share interactive ML demos directly on the Hub. Over time, huggingface_hub gained full programmatic control to deploy and manage Spaces (hardware requests, secrets, environment configuration, uploads). To deploy models on production-scale infrastructure, Inference Endpoints were integrated as well. Finally, the Jobs API came later (Q3 2025) to complete our compute offering.

The social and community layers became first-class citizens too: from APIs for pull requests and comments, to user and organization info, repository likes, following and followers, all the way through Collections to curate and share sets of related resources. Everyday ergonomics improved too: seamless authentication in Colab, resumable downloads, reliable uploads of large-scale folders, and more.

Then came version 0.28.0 and the Inference Providers ecosystem. Instead of a single inference backend, we partnered with multiple serverless providers (Together AI, SambaNova, Replicate, Cerebras, Groq, and more) to serve one API with transparent routing. We adopted a pay-per-request inference architecture that matched how people actually wanted to work.

Version 0.30.0 introduced Xet, a groundbreaking new protocol for storing large objects in Git repositories. Unlike Git LFS, which deduplicates at the file level, Xet operates at the chunk level (64KB chunks). When you update a large file in a dataset or a model, only the changed chunks are uploaded or downloaded, not the entire file.

The migration was massive, starting with 20 petabytes across over 500,000 repositories. Yet it happened transparently, with full backward compatibility. One year later, all 77PB+ over 6,000,000 repositories have been migrated to the Xet backend, allowing for much faster (and smarter!) uploads and downloads. This happened with no user intervention, and no disruption to existing workflows 🔥

Measuring the growth and impact of an open-source library is a tricky task. Numbers tell a story of their own:

But the real scale becomes clear when you look at the ecosystem. huggingface_hub is a dependency for over 200,000 repositories on GitHub and 3,000 packages on PyPI, powering everything from major third-party frameworks like Keras, LangChain, PaddleOCR, ChatTTS, YOLO, Google Generative AI, Moshi, NVIDIA NeMo, and Open Sora, to countless smaller libraries and tools across the ML landscape. Our own ecosystem (transformers, diffusers, datasets, sentence-transformers, lighteval, gradio, peft, trl, smolagents, timm, lerobot, etc.) benefits from this foundation as well.

The remarkable part? Most of the third-party integrations happened organically, and we played no role in them. The Hugging Face Hub empowers the ML community in countless ways, yet we're continually humbled by how far it has gone and how widely it's used.

Version 1.0 isn't just about reaching a milestone. It's about building the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. The breaking changes we've made aren't arbitrary; they're strategic decisions that position huggingface_hub to scale with the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on.

The most significant architectural change in v1.0 is our migration from requests to httpx. This isn't just dependency churn. It's a fundamental upgrade that brings the library into the modern era of HTTP.

Why httpx? The benefits are substantial: native HTTP/2 support for better connection efficiency and true thread safety that enables safe connection reuse across multiple threads. Most importantly, httpx provides a unified API for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, eliminating the subtle behavioral differences that existed between our sync and async inference clients.

The migration was designed to be as transparent as possible. Most users won't need to change anything. For those with custom HTTP backends, we've provided clear migration paths from configure_http_backend() to set_client_factory() and set_async_client_factory().

Additionally, hf_xet is now the default package for uploading and downloading files to and from the Hub, replacing the previously optional hf_transfer, which has now been fully removed.

Version 0.32.0 introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration and tiny-agents, fundamentally changing how developers build AI agents. What once required complex framework integration now takes approximately 70 lines of Python.

The MCPClient provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with tools, while the tiny-agents CLI lets you run agents directly from the Hub. Connect to local or remote MCP servers, use any Gradio Space as a tool, and build conversational agents that feel natural and responsive.

All of this is built on top of our existing InferenceClient and the dozens of Inference Providers it supports. We do believe Agents are the future, and huggingface_hub is there to provide the building blocks that enable AI builders to play with them.

The CLI has evolved from a simple command-line tool into a comprehensive interface for ML operations. The streamlined hf command replaces the legacy huggingface-cli with a modern resource-action pattern:

The CLI comes with a sandboxed installer, making it easy to upgrade without breaking existing dev environments:

With autocompletion support and an installer that works across platforms, the CLI now feels as polished as any modern developer tool.

Version 1.0 removes legacy patterns that were holding us back. The Git-based Repository class is gone. HTTP-based methods like upload_file() and create_commit() are simpler, more reliable, and better suited for modern workflows. The HfFolder token management has been replaced with explicit login(), logout(), and get_token() functions. The old InferenceApi class has been superseded by the more feature-complete InferenceClient. hf_transfer has been fully replaced by hf_xet binary package.

These changes weren't made lightly. Most deprecations were announced months in advance with clear warnings and migration guidance. The result is a cleaner, more maintainable codebase that can focus on forward-looking features rather than supporting deprecated patterns.

We understand that breaking changes are disruptive. That's why we've invested heavily in making the migration as smooth as possible. Our comprehensive migration guide provides step-by-step instructions for every change with explanations of why each change was necessary.

Most importantly, we've maintained backward compatibility wherever possible. HfHubHttpError, for example, inherits from both the old requests and new httpx base HTTPError classes, ensuring that error handling continues to work across versions. With this release, we're fully committing to the future and we will focus exclusively on v1.0 and beyond, ensuring we can deliver the performance, features, and tools the community needs to interact with the Hugging Face Hub. Previous v0.* versions will remain available on PyPI, but they will only receive vulnerability updates.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

To our 280+ contributors who built this library through code, documentation, translations, and community support, thank you!

We’re also deeply grateful to the entire Hugging Face community for their feedback, bug reports, and suggestions that have shaped this library.

Finally, a huge thank you to our users -from individual developers to large enterprises- for trusting huggingface_hub to power your workflows. Your support drives us to keep improving and innovating.

Please star us on GitHub ⭐ to show your support and help us continue building the foundation of open machine learning. It has been five years, but it is still only the beginning!
